summary: Doc in a Bag — Echo by AstroLogos is an offline-first crew-support prototype designed for situations where help, connectivity or sensor readings may be unavailable. It brings a conversational assistant, health records, equipment information, an offline medical library and interactive 3D anatomy into one workspace. Crew can use voice or text to navigate modules, inspect selected observations, explore spaceflight hazards and prepare a handoff for review. The system preserves measurement times, identifies stale or missing readings, and keeps fictional mission data separate from real wearable observations and research evidence. NASA resources inform its hazard explanations and mission-health context; they are not presented as astronaut telemetry. The current implementation runs on a Mac Studio, with a separate phone companion demonstrating limited local-model continuity. Our contribution is connecting records, references and actions around the crew member while keeping uncertainty visible. This is a working software prototype, not a clinically validated medical device or flight-ready emergency kit.
details:
Doc in a Bag is the portable-support concept; AstroLogos is the workspace, and Echo is its conversational interface. The question behind the project is practical: when Earth cannot answer immediately, what information and tools does the crew member still have?

The workspace brings together observations, health logs, equipment and inventory, offline references, interactive anatomy, mission replay, learning and handoff preparation. Echo accepts typed and spoken requests and connects supported commands to structured application actions. A crew member can select observation context, ask what is missing, open the heart in Human Atlas, highlight a spaceflight hazard, inspect its research source and prepare an unsaved handoff.

Our data model preserves who or what a record concerns, what was measured, the unit, observation time, source, mission phase and missingness. The research catalog contains 77 measurement concepts across nine mission stages; this is a design and evidence-coverage catalog, not 77 flight-validated sensors. Synthetic journey and benchmark records support repeatable software testing. Real wearable observations remain on a separate private local connection. A recent synchronization does not make an old measurement current, and missing values are never silently replaced with normal results.

Human Atlas uses reference anatomy from BodyParts3D. NASA's five spaceflight hazards provide research context for exploring relevant body systems. Selecting a structure does not diagnose an injury or prove exposure. Evidence cards distinguish what a source supports from what remains unknown. Handoff drafts retain their selected observations, timestamps and references and require review before any save or sharing.

The current workspace and local inference services run on a Mac Studio. The implementation uses React, TypeScript, Three.js, Python, SQLite and Kiwix-based offline content, with local speech recognition and speech output. Cloudflare provides protected remote access to the Studio-hosted workspace; it is separate from the local operating path. The accompanying phone demonstration shows a switch from Studio-assisted chat to an on-phone model while retaining a short conversation item. That limited test does not establish that every workspace module, medical model or emergency workflow runs independently on the phone.

We tested application navigation, source selection, synthetic evidence questions, Atlas interactions and unsaved handoff preparation, including local microphone workflows. Release tests checked password protection, denial of hosted wearable access and preservation of existing records. These are software and interaction tests, not clinical validation.

The intended benefit is less time switching among disconnected tools and a clearer account of what the crew knows, what is outdated and what must be handed over. Future work includes more capable portable hardware, workflow-specific model evaluation, improved device integration, accessibility under degraded conditions and review with medical and operational specialists. The bag shown in the presentation illustrates this future packaging; it is not a tested spaceflight medical kit.
